metadata.description: Learn ten skin changes worth checking, who may be at greater risk, how suspicious areas are assessed and what can happen after a diagnosis.
metadata.title: 10 Skin Cancer Warning Signs You Shouldn't Ignore

landing.title: 10 Skin Cancer Warning Signs You Shouldn't Ignore
landing.intro: Some are surprisingly easy to overlook — and several can appear in places people rarely check.

sections.title: 10 Skin Cancer Warning Signs You Shouldn't Ignore
sections.intro: Skin cancer can look different from one person to another. A change does not prove cancer, but a new, evolving or non-healing area should be assessed by a qualified healthcare professional.

points.title: A new spot or growth that does not go away
paragraphs: A new mark, lump or patch may appear and remain for weeks rather than settling like an ordinary irritation.
Many new skin changes are harmless, including bites, cysts and inflamed follicles. If the area persists, grows or keeps returning, arrange an assessment instead of trying to identify it yourself.

points.title: A mole that changes size, shape or colour
paragraphs: An existing mole may become larger, develop a different outline or show a noticeable change in colour over time.
Moles can alter for non-cancerous reasons, but evolution is one of the key melanoma warning patterns. Photographing the area for comparison can help you describe the change to a clinician.

points.title: One half looks different from the other
paragraphs: A suspicious pigmented mark can be asymmetrical, meaning its two halves do not match in shape or pattern.
Not every uneven mole is melanoma, and some melanomas do not follow a textbook pattern. New asymmetry or a visible change still warrants professional review.

points.title: An irregular, blurred or notched border
paragraphs: The edge of a mole or dark area may become ragged, poorly defined, scalloped or noticeably different from its previous outline.
Benign moles can have irregular edges too. The whole picture matters, particularly whether the border is changing or the mark looks unlike your other moles.

points.title: Uneven colour or several colours in one mark
paragraphs: A lesion may contain different shades of brown or black, or areas of red, pink, white or blue rather than one even colour.
Colour variation can occur in harmless lesions, while some melanomas have little pigment. A new or changing mix of colours should be checked rather than judged from appearance alone.

points.title: The ‘ugly duckling’ that looks unlike your other marks
paragraphs: One mole may stand out because it is darker, larger, shaped differently or simply does not resemble the pattern of your other moles.
Looking different is not a diagnosis, but it is a useful reason to take a closer look. A clinician can assess the outlier alongside the rest of your skin.

points.title: Itching, pain, oozing, crusting or bleeding
paragraphs: A mole or patch may start to itch, feel tender, form a crust, ooze or bleed without an obvious injury.
Eczema, friction, infection and scratching can cause similar symptoms. A repeated or unexplained change, especially in a mole, deserves assessment.

points.title: A sore that does not heal or keeps returning
paragraphs: A small sore may appear to improve and then break down, crust or bleed again in the same place.
Minor wounds should normally heal. A non-healing or repeatedly recurring sore can be a warning sign of basal-cell or squamous-cell skin cancer and should be examined.

points.title: A pearly bump or persistent rough, scaly patch
paragraphs: Non-melanoma skin cancers can appear as a shiny or translucent lump, a firm growth, or a red or skin-coloured patch that stays rough or scaly.
Common conditions such as eczema, psoriasis and benign growths can resemble these changes. Persistence, growth, bleeding or failure to respond as expected are reasons to seek advice.

points.title: A dark streak under a nail or a mark on a palm or sole
paragraphs: Some melanomas develop beneath a nail or on the palms and soles, including in areas that receive little sun. A new or widening dark nail streak can be one possible presentation.

Injury, infection and natural pigmentation are much more common explanations. These sites are important to check in every skin tone, and a changing or unexplained mark should be professionally assessed.

next.title: But Who Is Most At Risk?
next.copy: Skin changes are only part of the picture. UV exposure, personal history and several less obvious factors can affect a person's underlying risk.

sections.title: Skin Cancer Risk: 10 Things Worth Knowing
sections.intro: No single risk factor predicts who will develop skin cancer. Different types have different patterns, and people without obvious risk factors can still be diagnosed.

points.title: Ultraviolet exposure adds up
paragraphs: Ultraviolet radiation from the sun damages skin-cell DNA. Both intense intermittent exposure and years of cumulative exposure can contribute, depending on the type of skin cancer.

points.title: Repeated or severe sunburn
paragraphs: A history of blistering sunburn, particularly during childhood or adolescence, is linked with a higher melanoma risk. Avoiding further burns remains worthwhile at every age.

points.title: Indoor tanning
paragraphs: Sunbeds and tanning lamps expose skin to artificial ultraviolet radiation. They are not a safer alternative to sunlight and can increase skin-cancer risk.

points.title: Skin that burns easily
paragraphs: People with lighter skin, freckles, light eyes or red or blond hair often have less natural protection from ultraviolet radiation and may burn more readily. This raises risk but does not mean other skin tones are protected from skin cancer.

points.title: Many moles or unusual-looking moles
paragraphs: Having many moles or certain atypical moles can increase melanoma risk. Most moles never become cancer, so the important issue is the overall pattern and any change.

points.title: A previous skin-cancer diagnosis
paragraphs: Someone who has already had melanoma or another skin cancer can have a greater chance of developing another. Follow-up and self-check advice should be tailored to the individual diagnosis.

points.title: A close family history
paragraphs: Melanoma in close relatives can increase risk, particularly when several family members were affected or a recognised inherited syndrome is present. Most melanoma is not caused by a single inherited mutation.

points.title: A weakened immune system
paragraphs: Immune-suppressing medicines, organ transplantation and some medical conditions can raise the risk of certain skin cancers. The level of monitoring needed depends on the person's circumstances.

points.title: Age and long-term exposure
paragraphs: Many skin cancers become more common with age as the effects of ultraviolet exposure accumulate. Melanoma can still occur in younger adults, so age alone should never rule out assessment.

points.title: Skin cancer can affect every skin tone
paragraphs: Darker skin has more natural protection from ultraviolet radiation, but it does not make skin cancer impossible. Some melanomas in darker skin are found on the palms, soles or beneath nails and may be diagnosed later.
A new or changing lesion matters regardless of skin tone, sunburn history or where it appears. Risk information should guide awareness, not create false reassurance.

sections.title: What Actually Happens During A Skin Cancer Check?
sections.intro: A suspicious appearance is not a diagnosis. The assessment usually combines history, close examination and tissue testing when needed, and the exact pathway varies by lesion and location.

points.title: The change and your health history
paragraphs: A clinician may ask when the area appeared, how it has changed and whether it bleeds, itches or hurts. Sun exposure, previous skin cancers, medicines and family history can add useful context.

points.title: A close skin examination
paragraphs: The area is examined for its shape, colour, surface and other features. Depending on the concern, a clinician may also check the surrounding skin, other moles and nearby lymph nodes.

points.title: Dermoscopy
paragraphs: A dermatoscope is a handheld magnifying device with a light that reveals structures beneath the skin surface. It can help a trained clinician decide whether a lesion needs monitoring, removal or another assessment.

callouts.question: Does a suspicious-looking mark mean cancer?
callouts.answer: No. Many moles, growths and inflamed patches are benign, and appearance alone cannot confirm a diagnosis.

callouts.question: Can a blood test diagnose an early skin cancer?
callouts.answer: Usually not. Diagnosis generally relies on examining the skin and, when needed, testing a tissue sample.

callouts.question: Does every suspicious area need the same biopsy?
callouts.answer: No. The method depends on the suspected cancer type, size, depth, location and the clinician's judgement.

points.title: Photography, measurement or specialist referral
paragraphs: Some lesions are photographed or measured so change can be assessed over time. Features that raise concern can prompt referral to a dermatologist or specialist skin-cancer service.

points.title: Biopsy or removal where needed
paragraphs: A suspicious lesion may be partly sampled or removed so tissue can be examined under a microscope. When melanoma is suspected, removing the whole visible lesion is often preferred where clinically suitable, but individual approaches vary.

points.title: The pathology report
paragraphs: A pathologist identifies whether cancer is present and, if so, the exact type and other relevant features. Those details guide whether more surgery, staging tests or treatment discussions are needed.

sections.title: What Happens If Doctors Find Skin Cancer?
sections.intro: An abnormal result can describe several very different conditions. The next step depends on the exact diagnosis, how deeply it has grown, where it is and whether there is evidence of spread.

points.title: The result may still be benign
paragraphs: A biopsy can show a harmless mole, inflamed growth or another non-cancerous condition. The clinician may recommend no further treatment, routine observation or treatment for the underlying skin problem.

points.title: Precancerous or very early changes
paragraphs: Some reports identify abnormal cells confined to the top skin layer or a condition with potential to progress. Depending on the diagnosis, options can include removal, freezing, creams, light-based treatment or monitoring.

points.title: Basal-cell carcinoma
paragraphs: Basal-cell carcinoma is common and usually grows slowly. Treatment often aims to remove or destroy it locally, with the method influenced by its size, subtype and position.

points.title: Squamous-cell carcinoma
paragraphs: Squamous-cell carcinoma can behave more aggressively than basal-cell carcinoma and has a greater, though still limited, potential to spread. Pathology features and location help determine treatment and follow-up.

points.title: Melanoma is confirmed
paragraphs: The pathology report records features such as melanoma thickness and ulceration. Wider surgery around the original site is commonly discussed, and some people need lymph-node assessment or scans.

points.title: What stage and lymph-node findings mean
paragraphs: Stage describes how far the cancer has grown or spread. For melanoma, thickness, ulceration, lymph-node involvement and spread elsewhere are among the factors used to define stage and guide treatment.

points.title: The main treatment routes doctors may discuss
paragraphs: Surgery is central for many skin cancers. Depending on the type and stage, other options may include specialised surgery, topical or light-based treatments, radiotherapy, immunotherapy or targeted medicines.
These treatments are not interchangeable. A specialist team weighs the diagnosis, likely benefit, side effects, general health and personal preferences before recommending a plan.

sections.title: Skin Cancer Outlook: What Really Matters
sections.intro: There is no single outlook for every skin cancer. Doctors interpret the exact type, pathology and extent of disease together rather than relying on one visual feature or statistic.

points.title: The exact type of skin cancer
paragraphs: Basal-cell carcinoma, squamous-cell carcinoma and melanoma have different usual behaviours and treatment pathways. A broad label such as ‘skin cancer’ is not enough to predict what happens next.

points.title: Whether it is localised
paragraphs: Cancer confined to its original skin site generally offers more straightforward local treatment options than disease involving lymph nodes or distant organs.

points.title: Melanoma thickness
paragraphs: For melanoma, the measured depth of the tumour is a major staging and outlook factor. Greater thickness can be associated with a higher risk of spread.

points.title: Ulceration and other pathology features
paragraphs: The pathology report can describe whether the tumour surface is ulcerated and record other microscopic details. These findings help specialists understand biological behaviour.

points.title: Lymph-node involvement
paragraphs: Cancer cells found in nearby lymph nodes change the stage and can influence recommendations for surgery, medicines, imaging and follow-up.

points.title: Whether it has spread elsewhere
paragraphs: Distant spread changes treatment aims and outlook. Modern immunotherapies and targeted medicines have expanded options for some people with advanced melanoma, but responses vary.

points.title: Whether it was completely removed
paragraphs: Pathology can show whether cancer reaches an edge of the removed tissue. Further surgery may be recommended to achieve an appropriate clear margin, depending on the diagnosis.

points.title: Response to treatment, age and general health
paragraphs: Follow-up examinations, symptoms and scans can show how treatment is working. General health affects which options are suitable and how well treatment may be tolerated.

points.title: Why statistics cannot predict one person's future
paragraphs: Survival figures describe groups of people diagnosed in the past. They cannot account perfectly for one person's tumour biology, health, response to treatment or access to newer therapies.

conclusion.copy: Skin cancers can behave very differently from one another. A photograph, symptom or single risk factor cannot establish a diagnosis or an individual's outlook. New, changing or non-healing skin changes should be professionally assessed, and doctors combine examination, pathology and any staging information before discussing what happens next.
